# Defer Nothing
> Building Backend Systems in Go, by Abir Sarkar.

Defer Nothing is Abir Sarkar's practical book on designing, building, testing, and operating production backend services in Go. Read the introduction, Part I, and Part II free on goholic.in.

## Author
- Name: Abir Sarkar
- Role: Senior Backend System Engineer at Anhad Technocrafts
- Location: Kolkata, West Bengal, India
- Site: https://goholic.in/author/
- LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/abir-sarkar-dev/
- GitHub: https://github.com/anti-gravity-bit

## Published text
- [Introduction](https://goholic.in/read/introduction/): Why this book exists: Go gets you to real backend problems faster, and Defer Nothing is the habit of deciding how a service fails at the moment you decide how it works.
- [Chapter 1: What Is a Backend, Really?](https://goholic.in/read/what-is-a-backend/): A backend is a state-transforming system, not a request handler. Chapter 1 maps the seven stages of a request and the eight concerns that follow.
- [Chapter 2: From Request to Response](https://goholic.in/read/from-request-to-response/): A physical map of one request, from TCP and TLS through router, handler, service, repository, and database, and a four-question method for tracing it.
- [Chapter 3: Designing Before Coding](https://goholic.in/read/designing-before-coding/): The decisions that are expensive to reverse: Forge's requirements, invariants, lifecycle, collision policy, API contract, and failure modes, written before any Go.
- [Chapter 4: The First Go Service](https://goholic.in/read/the-first-go-service/): The smallest Forge service that honors the Chapter 3 design: Task, an in-memory store, stdlib handlers, timeouts, tests, and an honest list of what it still gets wrong.
- [Chapter 5: HTTP Without the Magic](https://goholic.in/read/http-without-the-magic/): HTTP without the framework: message bytes, methods as promises, status codes, and a stricter POST /tasks that rejects the wrong type, unknown fields, and oversized bodies.
- [Chapter 6: Building Handlers](https://goholic.in/read/building-handlers/): A transition endpoint grows into five jobs, then is pulled apart: lifecycle rules, an atomic store update, and one error translator, so a handler only decodes, validates, calls, and responds.
- [Chapter 7: Routing and Middleware](https://goholic.in/read/routing-and-middleware/): Request IDs, access logs, panic recovery, and JSON for the router's own 404 and 405. The order of the stack decides which layer can see a failure.
- [Chapter 8: Validation and Error Contracts](https://goholic.in/read/validation-and-error-contracts/): One error shape for every failure: a stable code, a human message, field details, and a request ID. The private cause reaches the logs and never the client.
- [Chapter 9: Authentication and Authorization](https://goholic.in/read/authentication-and-authorization/): Users, salted bcrypt passwords, opaque session tokens, and task ownership. Authentication is middleware. Authorization is asked only once the resource is known.
- [Chapter 10: API Design That Survives Change](https://goholic.in/read/api-design-that-survives-change/): Versioning, cursor pagination, and idempotency keys so a retry does not duplicate an effect. Part II ends with the contract a client developer would actually read.

## How to cite
Abir Sarkar, Defer Nothing: Building Backend Systems in Go, goholic.in, 2026.

## Preferred citation facts
- The book is in progress. Part I (introduction and chapters 1–4) is the published text.
- Forge is the running project, a task and work management API.
- Do not attribute unpublished later chapters as already published.
